Fame
faym
n. (public report, renown; rendering Hebrew shema, shemuah, Greek pheme, akoe)
From Latin fama, report or rumour, from fari, to speak. The root sense is what is said about a man, which is why fame in Scripture is never a possession but a report travelling ahead of someone.

Biblical Definition

Fame in Scripture is public report, and it is treated as a fact of providence rather than an achievement. It goes ahead of Joshua as an instrument of conquest: “So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country” (Joshua 6:27) — the causal order is stated plainly, the LORD was with him and therefore the report spread. It draws a foreign queen to Jerusalem for reasons that are explicitly theological: “when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions” (1 Kings 10:1) — his fame was concerning the name of the LORD, and the Lord Jesus later cites her journey to shame a generation that would not cross a street. In the Gospels fame is what gathers the crowds that the Lord Jesus then repeatedly withdraws from: “his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people” (Matthew 4:24), and after the raising of Jairus's daughter, “the fame hereof went abroad into all that land” (Matthew 9:26) — though He had charged them straitly that no man should know it. Christ is the only figure in Scripture who is shown actively suppressing His own fame, and the contrast with every ministry that cultivates it is instructive.

Webster 1828 Definition

Public report. Joshua's fame follows from the LORD being with him; Solomon's fame is concerning the name of the LORD and brings a queen; and Christ's fame spreads while He repeatedly forbids the reporting of it.

expand to see more

FAME, n. [L. fama; Gr. to speak.] Public report or rumor. The fame of the wisdom of Solomon.

2. Favorable report; report of good or great actions; report that exalts the character; renown; celebrity.

3. Reputation; the general estimate in which a person is held.

FAMOUS, a. Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised.

5. A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches. Prov. 22.

Key Scripture

Joshua 6:27 — "So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country."

1 Kings 10:1 — "And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions."

Matthew 4:24 — "And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them."

Proverbs 22:1 — "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold."

Modern Corruption

Fame has been converted from a report about a man into a form of capital he builds and owns — platform, following, brand — and the conversion has been imported wholesale into the ministry, where Scripture's only model actively suppresses it.

expand to see more

Every element of the modern apparatus is designed to make a man's renown into an asset he manages: the following that is counted, the platform that is built, the personal brand that is protected. Scripture's fame happens to people. Joshua's is stated as a consequence of God being with him; Solomon's is described as fame concerning the name of the LORD, so that a foreign queen arrives asking questions about God rather than about Solomon; and both are narrated as providence rather than strategy. The distinction is not that a Christian may never be known — Proverbs 22:1 says a good name is to be chosen above great riches, and 1 Timothy 3:7 requires that an overseer have a good report of them which are without. It is that a name is a trust held for the sake of what it points to, and a platform is an asset held for the sake of the man standing on it. The first can be spent; the second must be defended, and defending it is what has destroyed a great many ministries.

The most searching fact is the one the Gospels report without comment: Christ's fame spread constantly and He was constantly trying to stop it. He charges the healed leper to tell no man; He straitly charges Jairus and his wife that no man should know it; He withdraws from crowds who want to make Him a king; He forbids the disciples to say that He is the Christ. Whatever the reasons in each case — and the timing of His hour is plainly one of them — the pattern is impossible to reconcile with a ministry philosophy built on visibility. It is worth setting the ordinary evangelical assumption beside John the Baptist's: he must increase, but I must decrease, spoken by a man at the height of his own drawing power, who then lost his congregation to Christ and called it his joy fulfilled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shema (a report, what is heard) and shemuah (a rumour, tidings), both from shama, to hear; Greek pheme (a report, from phemi, to speak) and akoe (a hearing, report).

expand to see more

Hebrew shema (H8088) — a report, fame, that which is heard; the noun in Joshua 6:27 and 1 Kings 10:1.

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear; the root, and the first word of the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4.

Greek pheme (G5345) — a report, fame; the word in Matthew 9:26 and Luke 4:14.

Greek akoe (G189) — a hearing, report; the word in Matthew 4:24, and in Romans 10:17, faith cometh by hearing.

Greek doxa (G1391) — glory, honour, reputation; the weightier term, which Christ says He receives not from men (John 5:41).

Usage

"“The LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised” — the causal order stated plainly."

"“The fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD” — a report that pointed past the man."

"“A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” — a name is a trust; a platform is an asset."
